proposed_edges.relationship: In “Rethinking Military Revolutions” (2020), Black criticizes Parker’s military-revolution argument for selective evidence and for making the Low Countries a model of worldwide military change.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Freshly read on The Critic’s own site: paragraphs beginning “The usefulness of a concept”, “In my Beyond the Military Revolution”, and “So also with Parker following Rogers”. Black calls Parker’s evidence “highly selective” and objects to treating the Low Countries as a “paradigm for the entire world”. This answers the earlier tq_geoffrey_parker_black access hold: the article body is now readable through the web tool. Black’s books and Parker’s 2019 lecture remain unread; the criticism and account of that lecture remain Black’s.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Military Revolutions, Past and Present” and “Random Thoughts of a Hedgehog” (2003), Parker challenges Black’s organizational explanation and argues that examples of Western military failure do not explain the larger pattern of Western expansion.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read journal website excerpts, sections under these two titles: opening essay passages containing “Most recently” and “I contend”; rejoinder paragraphs beginning “Jeremy Black’s desire”, “Thus although”, and “Likewise”. Parker contrasts “advances in research and technology” with “military organization”, then argues against Black’s counterexamples. Black’s intervening “On Diversity and Military History” was also read. The website marks omissions with ellipses; complete print essays and Black’s books remain unread. This directed reply differs from Black’s incoming critique.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Homage to Braudel” (1980), Parker criticizes Civilisation matérielle, économie et capitalisme for neglecting war’s economic and social effects and questions whether international trade can bear its explanatory weight.
proposed_edges.map_label: War omitted; trade’s explanatory weight questioned, 1980
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Parker’s own review, London Review of Books 2:17, 4 September 1980. Exact locators: paragraphs beginning “Braudel’s argument will not please everyone” through “But was it really so in pre-industrial Europe?” He finds “no sustained discussion” of war’s consequences and doubts that trade explains European prosperity. Closing paragraphs beginning “In the long term” and “Braudel is a far better historian” retain his high praise. Braudel’s volumes were not read; Parker’s quantitative estimate is not independently verified or adopted.

proposed_edges.relationship: In his Itinerario interview (1997), Parker explicitly applies Kuhn’s paradigm concept to explain early modern statesmen’s persistence in policies despite information that contradicts them.
proposed_edges.map_label: Kuhn’s paradigm applied to policy persistence, 1997
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh primary reading in the authorized 2017 reprint, World History – a Genealogy, printed p. 53: after describing selective acceptance of information as “irrational consistency”, Parker names Kuhn’s Structure of Scientific Revolutions and extends the difficulty of recognizing a failed “paradigm” from scientists to statesmen. Note 2, p. 64, cites a 1971 edition. Cambridge’s original-article metadata verifies Itinerario 21:2 (July 1997), pp. 8–19; 2011 is digitization, 2017 the anthology. Kuhn’s book and original journal pagination were not freshly read. Influence means this explicit conceptual application.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Crisis of the Seventeenth Century” (Winter 2014), de Vries argues that Parker’s Global Crisis (2013) needs comparative measurement and a clearer distinction between long-term climatic change and short-term weather variability.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read de Vries’s own review article in the University of Warwick teaching share: p. 372 calls for “comparative and quantitative evidence”; p. 373 considers demographic variation and alternative explanations; pp. 376–377 criticize the substitution of narrative for “measurement and testing”. Pages 369–370 praise Parker’s achievement. Original issue: Journal of Interdisciplinary History 44:3 (Winter 2014), pp. 369–377; the footer’s 2013 copyright is recorded separately. Parker’s book and the demographic data were not independently read or checked.
